newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening lower, techs set to slump.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening lower, techs set to slump.

text.p: Wall Street is expected to open lower Friday, hurt by a slump in tech stocks, after giant software company Microsoft Corp posted fourth-quarter results which were seen as somewhat disappointing.

Weakness in the technology sector, whose recent power has helped the broader equities market rise, would likely drag both the Nasdaq composite and the Dow industrials down, analysts said. Both indices also closed lower yesterday.

"With Microsoft down in Europe, we are probably looking for the (Nasdaq) composite to open weaker, which could put some strain on the Dow," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said.
But while a slide in Microsoft shares may dampen enthusiasm for the tech sector, it should not cause wreak widespread damage in the broader stock market, analysts said.

"There will be some skittishness, some selling, but today's option expiry will lend some support and liquidity to markets," George Rodriguez, senior vice president of equities at Guzman & Co said. "Microsoft alone will not kill techs."

Microsoft reported fourth quarter earnings of $1.05 billion or $0.80 per share compared with $559 million or $0.43 per share a year earlier. Revenues rose 41 percent to $3.18 billion from $2.26 billion.

The company's earnings were a penny above the First Call consensus earnings estimate of $0.79 per share but below so-called "whisper numbers" that ran as much as $0.10 to $0.13 per share ahead of that estimate.
"Microsoft was something of a disappointment, my guess is because the company did not surprise the Street with a bigger percentage gain, as it has in the past," Cardillo said.
Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said: "Microsoft will soften enthusiasm for the techs but I don't think it is going to slam them."
Before the opening bell, Microsoft shares were trading at 143-3/4, down from a close of 149-8/16.
The Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was down 2.65 points at 935.30. The long bond was down 8/32 at 6.51 percent.
Among today's economic data, the Commerce Department reported that the U.S. trade gap widened 17 percent in May to $10.23 billion. It was forecast at $9.18 billion.

The dollar drifted down against the yen in Tokyo, trading at 115.68/78. In Europe, the dollar spiked up against the mark after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the recent strength in the dollar was not "earth-shattering."
It was trading at 1.7976/86 marks there.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 269.93 points, or 1.32 percent, at 20,249.32. Stocks finished lower there as traders squared positions ahead of a three-day weekend.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off 21.3 at 4927.7.
U.S. stocks were lower in London trading, hit by profit-taking in the technology sector.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that a recent profit warning by MCI Communications Corp has raised concerns about how British Telecommunications Plc can complete its planned acquisition of the U.S. telecommunications company without infuriating shareholders.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that the apparent management crisis at AT&T Corp has raised larger questions for the company.
((Wall Street desk 212-859-1730))
